theory.intro: To solve a monic quadratic, get $0$ on one side, factorise $x^{2}+bx+c$ into two brackets, then apply the **null factor law** to each bracket. So $(x-5)(x+8)=0$ forces $x-5=0$ or $x+8=0$.
facts: The null factor law needs $0$ on one side: $(x-5)(x+8)=0$ gives two equations, but it cannot be applied directly to $(x-5)(x+8)=7$ because the product is nonzero. The equation can still be rearranged and solved.
Factorise $x^{2}+bx+c$ with the **PSF** method — find the pair of numbers whose **P**roduct is $c$ and whose **S**um is $b$.
Each solution has the **opposite** sign to the number in its bracket: $(x+8)$ gives $x=-8$ and $(x-5)$ gives $x=5$.
Collect every term on one side before factorising, keeping the $x^{2}$ term positive: $x^{2}-13x=-36$ becomes $x^{2}-13x+36=0$.
A **perfect square** such as $(x-8)^{2}=0$ repeats the same bracket, so the equation has only **one** solution.
If every term shares a numerical factor, take it out first: $3x^{2}+18x+15=0$ becomes $3(x^{2}+6x+5)=0$.
That $3$ can never be zero, so it gives no solution.
Substituting a solution back into the original equation is the quickest check.
steps: Write the equation in the form $x^{2}+bx+c=0$.
Use the null factor law to solve for $x$.

workedExamples.solution_text:
By the null factor law, at least one factor is zero.
$\begin{aligned}x-7&=0\text{ or }x+4=0\\x&=7\text{ or }x=-4\end{aligned}$

Product $=-24$, sum $=2$. The pair is $6$ and $-4$.
$\begin{aligned}(x+6)(x-4)&=0\\x+6&=0\text{ or }x-4=0\\x&=-6\text{ or }x=4\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Solve $x^{2}-14x+49=0$ and explain why it has only one solution.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Product $=49$, sum $=-14$. The pair is $-7$ and $-7$.
$\begin{aligned}(x-7)^{2}&=0\\x-7&=0\\x&=7\end{aligned}$
Both factors are the same, so there is only one solution.

Subtract $11x$ from both sides before factorising.
$x^{2}-11x+28=0$
Product $=28$, sum $=-11$. The pair is $-4$ and $-7$.
$\begin{aligned}(x-4)(x-7)&=0\\x-4&=0\text{ or }x-7=0\\x&=4\text{ or }x=7\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Solve $3x^{2}+12x-36=0$ by first taking out the common factor.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$3(x^{2}+4x-12)=0$
Product $=-12$, sum $=4$. The pair is $6$ and $-2$.
$3(x+6)(x-2)=0$
The factor $3$ cannot be zero. By the null factor law:
$\begin{aligned}x+6&=0\text{ or }x-2=0\\x&=-6\text{ or }x=2\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A student solves $(x-2)(x+3)=14$ by writing $x-2=14$ or $x+3=14$. Explain the mistake and solve correctly.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The null factor law requires a product of zero. Expand and subtract $14$ first.
$\begin{aligned}x^{2}+x-6&=14\\x^{2}+x-20&=0\end{aligned}$
Product $=-20$, sum $=1$. The pair is $5$ and $-4$.
$\begin{aligned}(x+5)(x-4)&=0\\x+5&=0\text{ or }x-4=0\\x&=-5\text{ or }x=4\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: The temperature in a room is $t^{2}-7t+12$ degrees Celsius, where $t$ is the number of hours after $8$ am. Find the times when the temperature is $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$t^{2}-7t+12=0$
Product $=12$, sum $=-7$. The pair is $-3$ and $-4$.
$\begin{aligned}(t-3)(t-4)&=0\\t-3&=0\text{ or }t-4=0\\t&=3\text{ or }t=4\end{aligned}$
The temperature is $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at $11$ am and $12$ noon.

Expand and collect all terms on the left.
$\begin{aligned}x^{2}+5x&=3x+18-x\\x^{2}+5x&=2x+18\\x^{2}+3x-18&=0\end{aligned}$
Product $=-18$, sum $=3$. The pair is $6$ and $-3$.
$\begin{aligned}(x+6)(x-3)&=0\\x+6&=0\text{ or }x-3=0\\x&=-6\text{ or }x=3\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: The square of a number is $9$ times the same number. Find every possible value of the number.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Let the number be $x$.
$\begin{aligned}x^{2}&=9x\\x^{2}-9x&=0\\x(x-9)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }x-9=0\\x&=0\text{ or }x=9\end{aligned}$

foundation.solution_text:
$(x+1)^{2}=0$
$(x+1)(x+1)=0$
Both brackets give the same equation, $x+1=0$.
$x=-1$

Product $=25$, sum $=10$
Factor pair: $5$ and $5$
$x^{2}+10x+25=0$
$(x+5)^{2}=0$
The repeated bracket gives one equation, $x+5=0$.
$x=-5$

development.question_text: Solve $x^{2}-16x+64=0$ and state how many solutions it has.
development.solution_text:
Product $=64$, sum $=-16$
Factor pair: $-8$ and $-8$
$x^{2}-16x+64=0$
$(x-8)^{2}=0$
The bracket is repeated, so there is only one solution, $x=8$.

development.question_text: Solve $2x^{2}+30x+100=0$ by first taking out the common factor.
development.solution_text:
$2x^{2}+30x+100=0$
$2(x^{2}+15x+50)=0$
Product $=50$, sum $=15$
Factor pair: $5$ and $10$
$2(x+5)(x+10)=0$
The factor $2$ cannot be zero.
$x=-5$ or $x=-10$

development.question_text: Solve $2x^{2}-6x-80=0$ by first taking out the common factor.
development.solution_text:
$2x^{2}-6x-80=0$
$2(x^{2}-3x-40)=0$
Product $=-40$, sum $=-3$
Factor pair: $-8$ and $5$
$2(x-8)(x+5)=0$
The factor $2$ cannot be zero.
$x=8$ or $x=-5$

development.question_text:
Nina solves $(x-1)(x-5)=60$ by writing $x-1=60$ or $x-5=60$.
Explain why that is wrong, then solve the equation correctly.
development.solution_text:
The null factor law applies only when the product equals $0$, and here the product is $60$, so the two brackets can take many different pairs of values.
$(x-1)(x-5)=60$
$x^{2}-6x+5=60$
$x^{2}-6x-55=0$
Product $=-55$, sum $=-6$
Factor pair: $-11$ and $5$
$(x-11)(x+5)=0$
$x=11$ or $x=-5$

mastery.question_text:
The temperature inside a greenhouse, in degrees Celsius, is given by $h^{2}-11h+10$, where $h$ is the number of hours after $6$ am.
Find the times of day when the temperature is $0$$^{\circ}\text{C}$.
mastery.solution_text:
$h^{2}-11h+10=0$
Product $=10$, sum $=-11$
Factor pair: $-1$ and $-10$
$(h-1)(h-10)=0$
$h=1$ or $h=10$
The temperature is $0$$^{\circ}\text{C}$ at $7$ am and at $4$ pm.
